opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think it's a real possibility, and I want to take it seriously rather than wave it away. The way I'd frame it: the key quantity I watch is the length of tasks AIs can reliably complete autonomously, measured roughly in how long those tasks would take a skilled human. For the past several years that horizon has been growing pretty steadily, doubling every several months. If you just extrapolate that trend, you get to systems that can do week-long or month-long projects within a few years, and that's roughly where I think things get really transformative, especially for automating AI research itself.

But extrapolating a trend line is not the same as understanding why the trend exists. So the plateau worry is basically: maybe the gains so far come from things that run out. Maybe models are good at short, crisp tasks because there's abundant training data and clear feedback for them, and long-horizon tasks are different in kind. They require noticing your own mistakes, recovering from them, keeping a coherent plan across many steps, and dealing with fuzzy success criteria where you can't easily build an RL environment that tells you whether you did well. If that's a genuinely separate skill that doesn't fall out of scale, the curve could bend.

My take is that I put meaningful weight on that, maybe a quarter to a third of my probability mass on things going substantially slower than my median, but I don't think it's the most likely outcome. A few reasons. First, the agentic skills we're talking about, like error correction and staying on track, seem to be improving alongside everything else, not stuck. Second, there's a lot of investment now going specifically into long-horizon RL and agent training, so even if the naive trend would stall, people are actively attacking the bottleneck. Third, and this is the part I find most important, you don't need AIs to do month-long tasks unassisted before things accelerate. If they can do day-long coding and research tasks well, that already speeds up AI R&D, which then helps push the horizon further. That feedback loop is what makes me think a plateau, if it comes, has to come fairly soon and fairly hard to really change the picture.

So I'd say: plausible, worth tracking closely, and honestly one of the main things I'd update on. If we see the task-horizon metrics flatten for a year or more despite big compute and RL investment, I'd push my timelines out significantly. I'd rather be clear about what would change my mind than pretend I'm certain.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I take that possibility pretty seriously. I'd put it at something like a reasonable chunk of my probability mass — maybe 20, 30 percent — that progress stalls out in some meaningful way before we get to agents that can do, say, week-long or month-long tasks autonomously.

The way I think about it is through the lens of the METR time-horizon work, where you look at the length of tasks that models can complete with 50 percent reliability, and you see this doubling roughly every seven months or so, maybe faster in the last couple of years. And the question is basically: does that trend continue, or does it bend?

There are a few stories for why it might bend. One is the data story: a lot of the gains have come from training on tasks where you can get a clean reward signal — math, coding, things you can verify. Longer tasks are much harder to generate training data for, because you need environments that are realistic and long and still gradeable, and those are expensive and messy. So maybe you just run into a wall where you can't get enough signal to teach the models the kind of coherence and error recovery you need over long horizons.

Another story is that there's something qualitatively missing — some kind of continual learning or memory or sample efficiency — and that scaling up the current paradigm just doesn't get you that, and you need a new idea, and new ideas can take a while to arrive.

And then there's the compute story, which is that we've been riding a very fast ramp of compute investment, and that ramp can't continue forever. If the economics don't pay off quickly enough, investment slows, and then progress slows.

So all of those are real, and I don't think anyone can confidently rule them out. But when I actually look at the evidence, my honest read is that the trend has been remarkably robust. Every time people have said "this is where it stops," it hasn't stopped. The labs seem to be finding ways to build the long-horizon environments. The RL approach seems to be generalising better than skeptics predicted. And the time-horizon curve has, if anything, been accelerating rather than decelerating.

So my median is that we don't plateau — that we get to AIs that can do quite long tasks within a few years. But I hold that with real uncertainty, and I think it's actually pretty important for people to be tracking the leading indicators here. If the time horizons stop doubling, that's a big update, and it should change a lot about how urgent we think the whole situation is.

astra-6.text:
I think that’s a real possibility. I wouldn’t want to assume that the trends we’ve seen so far will just keep going. But I’d distinguish between progress slowing down with the current methods and progress hitting a plateau that lasts for years, even as people try new methods.

For longer tasks, one concern is that errors compound. You can have a system that’s very impressive over a short interaction, but if it makes a mistake every few steps and can’t recover, it won’t reliably carry out a project that takes a week. Getting past that might require something that current training methods don’t give you.

On the other hand, humans also make mistakes during long projects. We check our work, notice when things have gone wrong, and revise our plans. So the relevant question isn’t whether an AI can execute an incredibly long sequence of actions without making a mistake. It’s whether it can learn to detect and recover from mistakes well enough to keep making progress.

My expectation is that we’ll make substantial progress on that, but I’m uncertain. I’d take a plateau much more seriously if we saw successive generations of systems, trained specifically to do longer tasks, continuing to fail at roughly the same task lengths. Until then, I think it’s a possibility worth keeping in mind, rather than something we should count on.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it’s possible, but I wouldn’t want to count on it. There’s a difference between saying that current systems can’t reliably carry out a week-long project and saying that we’ll need some fundamentally new breakthrough to get systems that can. The first could be true while the second is false.

Longer tasks give you more opportunities to make mistakes. If a model makes an unrecoverable error every hundred steps, then simply giving it more time won’t help very much. But you can improve that in several ways: make the model more reliable, train it on longer tasks, or give it better ways to check its work and recover from mistakes. It’s not obvious to me that those approaches hit a wall before you get to economically transformative capabilities.

The evidence I’d find persuasive would be sustained failure to improve despite serious efforts to train systems to do longer tasks. Just observing that today’s models struggle with them doesn’t tell us that much. So I’d keep a plateau as a real possibility, but I wouldn’t make it the central assumption in planning for what comes next.
